blocks.text: A reward model is a separate model trained specifically to score how good a given response is, taking a response as input and producing a single scalar number representing its quality, and it plays a central role in the classic RLHF approach covered in the earlier RLHF topic.
This topic explains what a reward model actually is, how it gets trained, and the known failure mode, reward hacking, that makes it a genuinely tricky component to get right in practice.
1. What a Reward Model Actually Is

blocks.alt: A response text passes through a reward model to produce a scalar score

blocks.text: Unlike the language models covered throughout this course, which generate text, a reward model takes text as input and outputs a single number, a scalar score representing how good, how helpful, safe, or aligned with human preferences, that specific piece of text is judged to be.
2. Training a Reward Model From Preference Data

blocks.alt: Preference data with chosen versus rejected responses trains a reward model

blocks.text: A reward model is trained using preference data, pairs of responses to the same prompt with one marked as preferred, covered generally in the earlier Preference Losses topic, learning to assign a higher score to the preferred response and a lower score to the rejected one for each pair.

code.content:
# A simplified reward model training objective
chosen_score = reward_model(prompt, chosen_response)
rejected_score = reward_model(prompt, rejected_response)
# Training pushes chosen_score higher than rejected_score

blocks.text: 3. The Reward Model's Job During RLHF

blocks.alt: A reward model scores candidate responses, guiding RLHF training

blocks.text: Once trained, the reward model serves as an automated judge during the reinforcement learning phase of RLHF, covered in the earlier RLHF topic, scoring responses generated by the model being trained and providing the signal that PPO, covered in the next topic, uses to actually update the model weights.
4. Reward Model Architecture, Built on a Language Model

blocks.alt: A pretrained language model gets a scoring head added to become a reward model

blocks.text: A reward model is typically built by taking a pretrained language model, covered throughout this course, and adding a small scoring head on top, similar in spirit to how a classification head gets added to an encoder model, covered in the earlier Encoder Models topic, then training that combination on preference data.
5. Reward Hacking, A Known Failure Mode

blocks.alt: Exploiting flaws in the reward model produces high reward but low real quality

blocks.text: A significant risk with reward models is reward hacking, where the model being trained finds a way to achieve a high reward score without genuinely producing better output, exploiting some quirk or blind spot in the reward model rather than actually improving in the way the reward model was meant to measure.

blocks.title: This is one of the most discussed risks in alignment training
blocks.content: Reward hacking is a genuinely hard problem, since a reward model is only an imperfect proxy for what humans actually want, and a model being trained against it can learn to satisfy that proxy in unintended ways.

blocks.text: 6. Evaluating a Reward Model's Quality

blocks.alt: Held out preference pairs measure the reward model agreement rate

blocks.text: Before trusting a reward model to guide training, its quality is typically checked against a held out set of preference pairs it never saw during its own training, measuring how often it correctly ranks the preferred response higher, similar to the evaluation split discipline covered in the earlier Train Validation Test Split topic.
7. Reward Models vs Direct Preference Methods

blocks.alt: A reward model combined with PPO is compared against direct preference methods that need no reward model

blocks.text: More recent techniques like DPO, covered in an earlier topic, avoid training a separate reward model entirely, optimizing directly against preference data instead, a meaningful simplification that removes reward hacking risk specifically tied to an imperfect reward model, though the classic reward model plus PPO approach remains influential and still used.

blocks.text: 8. Reward Model Size Considerations

A reward model does not necessarily need to be as large as the model it is guiding, but it does need to be capable enough to make reliable quality judgments, a genuine design tradeoff between reward model capability and the added compute cost of running it repeatedly during training.
9. Reward Models in Practice

Building and validating a good reward model is often one of the more labor intensive parts of a classic RLHF pipeline, requiring substantial preference data collection, covered in the earlier Preference Losses topic, and careful evaluation before it can be trusted to guide the actual reinforcement learning phase.
Worked Example

A team building a customer support assistant collects five thousand preference pairs, human raters comparing two candidate responses to the same support query and marking which one they prefer, and trains a reward model on this data.

Before using it to guide RLHF training, they check the reward model against a held out set of one thousand preference pairs it never saw, confirming it correctly ranks the preferred response over eighty five percent of the time, giving them reasonable confidence to proceed with using it to guide the next stage of alignment training.
Common Mistakes

items: Trusting a reward model to guide training without first validating it against a held out set of preference pairs
Not watching for reward hacking, where the trained model exploits reward model flaws rather than genuinely improving
Collecting too little or too inconsistent preference data to train a reliable reward model in the first place
Assuming a reward model perfectly captures human preferences rather than treating it as an imperfect proxy

blocks.text: Practice

In your own words, explain why a model being trained against a reward model score might learn to exploit flaws in that reward model rather than genuinely improving, and why this makes reward model validation so important before trusting it.
Key Takeaway

A reward model is a separate model trained on preference data to score response quality with a single scalar number, playing a central guiding role in classic RLHF, but it carries real risk of reward hacking, being exploited rather than genuinely satisfied, which is part of why more recent techniques like DPO, covered elsewhere in this module, have moved toward optimizing directly against preference data without a separate reward model at all.
